items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the insurance law, in relation to notices to increase premium
rates for long-term care insurance
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4327

SPONSOR: MAYER
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to notices to increase
premium rates for long-term care insurance

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

To provide prospective buyers of long-term care insurance with estimates
of premium increases and other related information so that they can make
an informed decision based on estimated future financial impacts.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 requires insurers selling long-term care insurance to, before
the policy is executed, provide the prospective insured with a written
statement as to the anticipated good faith increases in premiums for the
policy in question over the next ten years and a graph showing past
premium rate increases over the previous ten years for such policy (or a
similar policy).

Section 2 requires insurers providing long-term care insurance to notify
policyholders when they file an application with the state to increase
premiums. The notice must include:

(i) a written statement as to the anticipated good faith increases in
premiums for the policy in question over the next ten years, a graph
showing past premium rate increases over the previous ten years for such
policy (or a similar policy); and

(ii) aggregated, anonymized data showing actions taken by past or other
current policyholders in response to proposed rate increases for similar
policies, including letting a policy lapse, decreasing policy benefits,
and accepting the proposed rate increase.

Section 3 provides the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Long-term care insurance can provide financial security later in life as
the daily cost of care increases cover the cost of care and daily activ-
ities that people may need as they age. Because other available options
do not pay for long term care, insurance to cover those costs helps
defray such expenses which would otherwise have to be paid out of pock-
et.

Unfortunately, the long-term care insurance industry has raised premiums
significantly and frequently. The increases are so substantial that many
policyholders are forced to drop the policy altogether. Many New Yorkers
who purchased these policies are understandably distressed to find that
they are paying premiums far higher than what they thought they would be
paying when they originally agreed to the policy.

This legislation helps consumers make better decisions about their
coverage at the time the policy is first executed and whenever there is
a premium increase by forcing long-term care insurers to provide esti-
mates of likely premium increases and information about how other simi-
larity situated customers have reacted to premium increases. This infor-
mation can help a prospective insured understand the likelihood of
premium increases and make a more informed decision about their finan-
cial future.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

None

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

A.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the insurance law, in relation to requiring certain notices be
posted and provided regarding long term care insurance policy changes
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4327A

SPONSOR: MAYER
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to requiring certain
notices be posted and provided regarding long term care insurance policy
changes

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

To increase transparency in the long-term care insurance premium rate
increase approval process by providing for additional communications to
insureds by the Department of Financial Services with respect to a rate
increase application, to require that the best interest of the policy-
holders be explicitly considered by the Department of Financial Services
when making a determination as to such application, and to require addi-
tional disclosures to policyholders by insurance companies.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 requires insurers requesting premium rate increases for long-
term care insurance to provide policyholders with a written statement as
to the good faith anticipated increases in premiums for the policy in
question over the next ten years, historical premium rate increases over
the previous ten years for such policy (or a similar policy), and a
notice that policyholders may publicly comment on the rate increase
application on the Department of Financial Services website.

Section 2 requires consideration of the best interests of policyholders
when the Department of Financial Services makes determinations as to
whether to approve, disapprove, or modify a premium rate increase appli-
cation.

Section 3 places requirements on both the Department of Financial
Services and insurers.

1. The Department of Financial Services under the provisions of Section
3 must:

(a) provide a publicly available summary of any application for a long
term care insurance premium rate increase;

(b) provide for 30 days of public comment on the rate increase applica-
tion on its website; and

(c) make public its written decision regarding approval, disapproval, or
modification of any premium rate increase application, including:  (i) a
summary of its determinations, and (ii) a written statement as to why
the decision is in the best interests of the policyholders.

2. Under the provisions of section 3, insurers providing long term care
insurance must notify policyholders when the Department of Financial
Services renders a decision on an application to increase premiums. The
notice must include:

(a) a description of the decision;


(b) the same information required by section 1 of the bill related to
likely future premium increases as well as historical increases; and

(c) aggregated, anonymized data showing actions taken by past or other
current policyholders in response to proposed rate increases for similar
policies, including letting a policy lapse, decreasing policy benefits,
and accepting the proposed rate increase.

Section 4 provides the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Long-term care insurance can provide financial security later in life as
the daily costs of care increases by covering the cost of care and
assistance with daily activities that people may need as they age.

Unfortunately, the long-term care insurance industry has raised premiums
significantly and frequently. Many New Yorkers who purchased these poli-
cies are understandably distressed to find that they are paying premiums
far higher than what they thought they would be paying when they
originally agreed to the policy. The increases are so substantial that
many policyholders are forced to drop their policies altogether. An
article in the New York Times on August 23, 2019, "Your Long-Term Care
Insurance Rate Spiked. Now
What?"(https://www.nytimes.com/2019/08/23/your-money/ long-term-care-in-
surance-prices.html) details the challenges of struggling to keep up
with skyrocketing premiums.

This legislation will give insureds more clarity and a stronger voice
when insurers seek premium increases by increasing transparency, requir-
ing additional background information, providing for public comment at
the time that rate increase applications are under consideration, and by
explicitly requiring the Department of Financial Services to consider
and publicly opine on the best interest of policyholders with respect to
the rate increase application in question.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

B.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4327B

SPONSOR: MAYER
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to requiring certain
notices be posted and provided regarding long term care insurance policy
changes

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

To raise the minimum loss ratio standard for premium increases for long-
term care insurance policies, to increase transparency in the long-term
care insurance premium rate increase approval process by providing for
additional communications to insureds by the Department of Financial
Services with respect to a rate increase application, to require that
the best interest of the policyholders be explicitly considered by the
Department of Financial Services when making a determination as to such
application, and to require additional disclosures to policyholders by
insurance companies.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 requires insurers requesting premium rate increases for long-
term care insurance to provide policy holders with a written statement
as to the good faith anticipated increases in premiums for the policy in
question over the next ten years, historical premium rate increases over
the previous ten years for such policy (or a similar policy), and a
notice that policy holders may publicly comment on the rate increase
application on the Department of Financial Services website.

Section 2 requires consideration of the best interests of policyholders
when the Department of Financial Services makes determinations as to
whether to approve, disapprove, or modify a premium rate increase appli-
cation.

Section 3 places requirements on both the Department of Financial
Services and insurers:

The Department of Financial Services under the provisions of Section 3
must
(a) provide a publicly available summary of any application for a long
term care insurance premium rate increase;
(b) provide for 30 days of public comment on the rate increase applica-
tion on its website; and
(c) make public its written decision regarding approval, disapproval, or
modification of any premium rate increase application, including:  (i) a
summary of its determinations, and (ii) a written statement as to why
the decision is in the best interests of the policy holders.

Under the provisions of section 3, insurers providing long term care
insurance must notify policy holders when the Department of Financial
Services renders a decision on an application to increase premiums.  The
notice must include
(a) a description of the decision;
(b) the same information required by section 1 of the bill related to
likely future premium increases as well as historical increases; and
(c) aggregated, anonymized data showing actions taken by past or other
current policyholders in response to proposed rate increases for similar
policies, including letting a policy lapse, decreasing policy benefits,
and accepting the proposed rate increase.

Section 4 requires the Department of Financial Services to ensure that
minimum loss ratios for long-term care premiums are no less favorable to
policy holders than the standards set by the National Association of
Insurance Commissioners' model regulations.

Section 5 provides the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Long-term care insurance can frequently provide financial security later
in life by mitigating the high financial burden of paying for increased
care that people may need as they age.  Unfortunately, the long-term
care insurance industry has raised premiums significantly and frequent-
ly. Many New Yorkers who purchased these policies are understandably
distressed to find that they are paying premiums far higher than what
they thought they would be paying when they originally agreed to the
policy. The increases are so substantial that many policy holders are
forced to drop their policies altogether. An article in the New York
Times on August 23, 2019, "Your Long-Term Care Insurance Rate Spiked.
Now What?"
(https://www.nytimes.com/2019/08/23/your-money/long-term-care- insu-
rance-prices.html) details the challenges of struggling to keep up with
skyrocketing premiums.

Among other improvements, this bill will make a significant change in
the determination of premium increases by requiring the Department of
Financial Services to ensure that the percentage of premiums received by
insurers that go to paying out benefits (the minimum loss ratio) is no
less favorable to policy holders than the percentage set forth in the
long-term care insurance model regulations published by the National
Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC). Currently, the minimum
loss ratios set by regulation in New York are 60% or 65% depending on
the age of the insured, regardless of whether the rate approval is in
connection with a new policy or a premium increase. In contrast, while
the NAIC model regulations stipulate a minimum loss ratio of 58% for new
policies (slightly lower than as set in New York's regulations), it also
sets a minimum loss ratio of 85% for any premium increases. Accordingly,
this bill will mean that 20%-25% more of premiums paid when rates are
increased will have to go towards paying out claims, thus bringing New
York in line with other states that have adopted the latest model regu-
lations. This is a major victory for New Yorkers who hold long term care
insurance policies and will put significant downward pressure on premium
increases.

In addition, this legislation will give insureds more clarity and a
stronger voice when insurers seek premium increases by increasing trans-
parency, requiring additional background information, providing for
public comment at the time that rate increase applications are under
consideration, and by explicitly requiring the Department of Financial
Services to consider and publicly opine on the best interest of policy-
holders with respect to the rate increase application in question.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill
 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

AN ACT to amend the insurance law, in relation to requiring certain notices be

C.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4327C

SPONSOR: MAYER
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to requiring certain
notices be posted and provided regarding long term care insurance policy
changes

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

To increase transparency in the long-term care insurance premium rate
increase approval process by providing for additional communications to
insureds by the Department of Financial Services with respect to a rate
increase application and the ability for public comment, to require that
the best interest of the policyholders be considered by the Department
of Financial Services when making a determination as to such applica-
tion, to require additional disclosures to policyholders by insurance
companies, and to ensure a high minimum loss ratio standard for premium
increases for longterm care insurance policies.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 requires insurers offering long-term care insurance to provide
prospective insureds with:

(a) a written statement as to whether the insurer anticipates requesting
increases in premiums for the policy in question over the next ten
years,

(b) historical premium rate increases over the previous ten years for
such policy (or a similar policy),

(c) contact information for DFS and the insurer,

(d) information about whether not the premium can increase, and if so,
under what circumstances,

(e) whether the policy contains any refund provisions,

(f) a description of ways to mitigate future premium increases,

(g) a description of policyholder options for surrendering the policy,

(h) a statement that the policyholder will have 60 days' written notice
before any premium increase,

(i) a statement that if the insurer seeks a premium increase, DFS will
post notice of the rate filing on its website, and

(j) notice that policyholders may publicly comment on the rate increase
application on the Department of Financial Services website.

Section 2 requires consideration of the best interests of policyholders
when the Department of Financial Services makes determinations as to
whether to approve, disapprove, or modify a premium rate increase appli-
cation.


Section 3 places requirements on both the Department of Financial
Services and insurers:

The Department of Financial Services under the provisions of Section 3
must

(a) make public any application for a long term care insurance premium
rate increase;

(b) post on its website the process it uses for reviewing and approving
premium rates;

(c) provide for 30 days of public comment on the rate increase applica-
tion on its website; and

(d) make public its written decision regarding approval, disapproval, or
modification of any premium rate increase application, including:  (i) a
summary of its determinations, and (ii) a written statement as to why
the decision is in the best interests of the policy holders.

Under the provisions of section 3, insurers providing long term care
insurance must notify policy holders when the Department of Financial
Services renders a decision on an application to increase premiums.  The
notice must include:

(a) a description of the decision; and

(b) the same information required by section 1 of the bill related to
the likelihood of future premium increases and historical increases.

Section 4 requires the Department of Financial Services to ensure that
minimum loss ratios for long-term care premiums are no less favorable to
policy holders than the standards set by the National Association of
Insurance Commissioners' model regulations.

Section 5 provides the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Long-term care insurance can provide financial security later in life by
mitigating the high financial burden of paying for increased care that
people may need as they age. Unfortunately, the long-term care insurance
industry has raised premiums significantly and frequently.  Many New
Yorkers who purchased these policies are understandably distressed to
find that they are paying premiums far higher than what they thought
they would be paying when they originally agreed to the policy. The
increases are so substantial that many policy holders are forced to drop
their policies altogether. An article in the New York Times on August
23, 2019, "Your Long-Term Care Insurance Rate Spiked.  Now
What?"(https://www.nytimes.com/2019/08/23/ your-money/long-termcare-
insur ance-prices.html) details the challenges of struggling to keep up
with skyrocketing premiums. To make matters worse, the process by which
insurers obtain approval from the Department of Financial Services for
premium increases is opaque and lacks all opportunity for policyholder
input.

This legislation will give insureds more clarity and a stronger voice
when insurers seek premium increases by increasing transparency, requir-
ing additional background information, providing for public comment at
the time that rate increase applications are under consideration, and by
explicitly requiring the Department of Financial Services to consider
and publicly opine on the best interest of policyholders with respect to
the rate increase application in question.

In addition, this bill will require that the determination of premium
increases by the Department of Financial Services ensure that the
percentage of premiums received by insurers that go to paying out bene-
fits (the minimum loss ratio) is no less favorable to policy holders
than the percentage set 'forth in the long-term care insurance model
regulations published by the National Association of Insurance Commis-
sioners (NAIC). Currently, the minimum loss ratios set by regulation in
New York are 60% or 65% depending on the age of the insured, regardless
of whether the rate approval is in connection with a new policy or a
premium increase. In contrast, while the NAIC model regulations stipu-
late a minimum loss ratio of 58% for new policies (slightly lower than
as set in New York's regulations), it sets a minimum loss ratio of 85%
for any premium increases.

Long-term care insurance will continue to pose financial challenges for
New Yorkers for a long time to come. However, this bill will eliminate
some of the current lack of information and disregard for consumer
participation so that the Department of Financial Services and the
insurers are forced to recognize that they are not the only two parties
involved in the premium rate increase process - the policyholder is the
third, and most important, party when it comes to any premium increase
filing - they are the ones actually paying the premiums, and they are
currently excluded from participating. This conduct by the Department of
Financial Services and insurers needs to change, and this bill is a
major step in the right direction.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
The act shall take effect 180 days after becoming law.

summary: Requires the superintendent of financial services to make public any rate filing or application submitted by long term care insurance carriers; requires certain notices be provided to policyholders and certificate holders regarding premium rate increases; requires the superintendent ensure the proper standard for minimum ratio losses when establishing minimum benefit standards.
